item.title: Tunable coupling between valley and magnetic excitons in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures
item.description:
Long shot new result — Discovered type-II band alignment and magnetic proximity coupling in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures, yielding enhanced Zeeman valley splitting and spin-selective interlayer charge transfer dependent on relative spin-valley polarization and CrSBr magnetization.

Grade 0.420 · 1.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Jianchen Dang, Liza Godziashvili, Kaichen Xie, Arun Ramanathan, Vadym Kulichenko, Alejandro Busto, Jia-Yi Ji, Robert Boyd, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Sina Najmaei, Daniel Rhodes, Luis Balicas, Xavier Roy, Ting Cao, Xiao-Xiao Zhang

Asks

How do magnetic order and anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr couple to valley excitons in monolayer WS2?

But

Dependent on twist angle and relative alignment between valley-spin polarization and magnetic substrate.

Tools

monolayer WS₂/CrSBr van der Waals heterostructures · circularly polarized photoluminescence spectroscopy · magneto-optical measurements

Abstract

Interfacial coupling in van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offers an effective route to tailor the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of materials. Versatile control and precise engineering of such interlayer interactions can be further achieved through external parameters, like electric field, magnetic field, optical excitation, as well as layer stacking geometries. Here, we examined the magneto-optical properties of 2D semiconductor heterostructures made of antiferromagnetic CrSBr and a monolayer WS2, both of which host intriguing excitonic properties. We identified a type-II band alignment between these two layers and the magnetic proximity effects from CrSBr, manifested by an enhanced Zeeman valley splitting in the WS2 layer. The interlayer charge transfer shows strong spin selectivity and is governed by the relative alignment between the valley-spin polarization of photoexcited carriers in WS2 and the magnetization in CrSBr, giving rise to spin-sensitive circularly polarized photoluminescence (PL) from WS2. Furthermore, the highly anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr enables stacking-dependent control of interlayer interactions, as inferred from a twist-angle dependence of PL quenching. Our work establishes a highly tunable 2D system that integrates valleytronics and magnetic excitons through multiple coupling channels, opening up new opportunities in all-optical manipulation of spin and magnon states and for the development of flexible spin-optoelectronic devices.

item.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
item.description:
Long shot new method — Demonstrates statistical quantum phase estimation on an analog simulator without auxiliary qubits, extracting absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in one- and two-dimensional arrays of up to N=19 Rydberg atoms.

Grade 0.402 · 1.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Hendrik Timme, Benjamin F. Schiffer, Ohad Lib, Shijia Sun, Maximilian Ammenwerth, Dominik S. Wild, J. Ignacio Cirac, Immanuel Bloch, Johannes Zeiher

Figure

Measured ground-state energy EGS/(NΩ) and separation to the first excited band versus detuning Δ/Ω for 5- and 19-atom chains, extracted from the Fourier transform of the reconstructed complex Loschmidt echo.

Asks

Can quantum phase estimation and complex-valued Loschmidt echoes be realized on an analog quantum simulator without controlled time evolution or ancilla registers?

But

Operates within the nearest-neighbor Rydberg blockade approximation (Vnn≫Ω,|Δ|); systematic phase error is 𝒪(τ2) after analytical initial-time bias subtraction, requiring nonzero echo amplitude.

Tools

Strontium-88 optical tweezer arrays · Clock-to-Rydberg transition (n=47 ³S₁) · Digital-analog imaginary-time evolution (ITE) protocol · Loschmidt echo phase reconstruction via Cauchy-Riemann relation · Statistical quantum phase estimation

Abstract

Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.

item.title: Optically-induced electric Aharonov-Bohm effect
item.description:
Long shot theory — Optical rectification of a 100 fs laser pulse inside a KTP crystal generates a quasi-DC field yielding an electric Aharonov-Bohm phase ϕAB=π at laser intensity I0≈4.3×108 W/cm2. The residual field inside the slit apertures is an order of magnitude smaller and displaces only the diffraction envelope without shifting the fringes.

Grade 0.399 · 1.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Gabriel P. Martins, Herman Batelaan, Pablo L. Saldanha

Figure

Electron interference intensity versus screen position y. Top panel demonstrates that local residual fields only shift the overall envelope, while bottom panel shows that increasing laser intensity shifts the interference fringes via the electric Aharonov-Bohm phase.

Asks

Can the electric Aharonov-Bohm effect be observed for free electrons traversing paths with negligible local electric fields?

But

Theoretical calculation in the paraxial approximation. Assumes electron position changes negligibly during the 100 fs pulse passage.

Tools

optical rectification · nonlinear optical crystal (KTP) · electron double-slit interferometer · ultrafast laser pulses

Abstract

Although it was proposed almost 70 years ago, the electric version of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect, where the interference pattern of quantum charged particles is affected by electric fields that do not interact locally with them, was never experimentally implemented. Here we propose a feasible way to experimentally verify such an important effect, for an electron double-slit interferometer with the slits carved in a nonlinear crystal. The AB phase is generated by a quasi-DC electric field induced in the crystal with the passage of a light pulse (the optical rectification effect) while the electron is superposed in the two slits. We show that this procedure can change the interference pattern of a ensemble of electrons even if they are subjected to negligible electric fields during their propagation, considering feasible parameters.
